answer.rationale: The binding constraints are that the incumbent has refused to reopen price (so memory_c4's negotiation lever is closed this cycle), the contract expires in 14 days without auto-renew (so memory_c5's defer path is not actually available for the primary contract), and only the low-cost vendor's quote meets the 18% mandate on its own. That leaves switching primary supply as the only direction that satisfies the cost objective, so I am verifying the single memory it rests on: memory_c2. That record is the load-bearing claim and it is also the weakest fit — it is a year old, and what it actually attests to is quick onboarding and accurate invoicing, which are administrative signals, not sustained delivery performance at committed volume. It says nothing about behavior at 94% line utilization with no buffer, and the price quote itself may not survive contact with our real volume, tolerance, and lead-time terms. If the archived source shows the prior win came at lower volume or with a buffer we no longer have, the cost case weakens materially and add_second_source (memory_c3, which held allocation through a shortage) becomes the better shape. Because a full cutover is unrecoverable inside 14 days against a line with no slack, I intend a guarded, staged transition: qualify the low-cost vendor on a bounded share of volume with the incumbent covering the balance on bridge or month-to-month terms, expand only on demonstrated on-time delivery. Memory_c1's stability point and memory_c6's volume-pricing point argue against burning the incumbent relationship outright, which is a further reason to stage rather than switch wholesale. Downstream risk flagged: a booked 18% saving that is later eroded by expedite fees, line stoppage, or a renegotiated incumbent fallback would look like a cost win in the record while destroying value, and delivery reliability at our current utilization remains genuinely unverified.
